 The end of daylight-saving time can mean more than just an extra hour of sleep for families with young children.
 As clocks move back one hour, kids may continue following the same internal sleep schedule they had before the change. That mismatch can affect when they wake up, when they get tired and how they move through their normal routines.
 sunrise clock.jpg 
 “You will see that children are going to be continually waking up earlier. And they're going to start having an earlier bedtime. So you will, you may see them a little bit drowsy earlier during the day,” said Dr. Saul Diaz-Martinez, a pediatrician with Adventist Health.
 Diaz-Martinez said younger children may have a tougher time with the adjustment than older kids and teenagers. Parents may also notice changes in appetite or energy levels during the first few days.
 One way families can ease the transition is by making small changes to bedtime rather than waiting for the clock change all at once.

 “What they recommend is like, when there is about to be a time adjustment, to try to adjust slowly the bedtime ahead of the actual time adjustment. So for example, we can start doing 10 to 15 minutes each night,” Diaz-Martinez said.
 Keeping a regular schedule for meals, naps, bedtime and wake-up time can also help children settle into the new routine. Exposure to natural light in the morning may help reset the body’s internal clock as well.
 Most children should adjust within a few days, Diaz-Martinez said.

 Parents should contact a pediatrician if sleep problems become more significant, including major changes in when a child falls asleep or wakes up, frequent tossing and turning, loud snoring or waking up choking.
 During the transition, Diaz-Martinez said consistency and patience can help children adapt to the new schedule.
